title: Taoism
summary: Taoism is one of the main traditions of Chinese thought, linked with the names of Laozi (the Tao Te Ching) and Zhuangzi. At its center is the Tao, “the Way”: a nameless natural order through which everything arises, changes and returns to its source. Wisdom, for the Taoists, lies in not forcing the nature of things but moving along with it, like water.
onEmotions: Taoists see feelings as part of life’s natural movement — like changes in the weather or the turning of the seasons: joy and sadness, rise and fall pass into one another, like yin and yang. Zhuangzi wrote that joy and anger, sorrow and delight, worry and regret follow one another day and night, and no one knows where they spring from. The trouble isn’t the feelings, but that we freeze up: we cling to one, wage war on another, judge ourselves by other people’s measures. The Taoist ideal is wu wei, “non-action” — that is, action without force or needless effort: letting a feeling flow, without inflating it or suppressing it.

anxiety.text: In the Zhuangzi, Confucius advises a student to practice the “fasting of the heart”: to listen not with the ears, nor even with the mind, but with the breath, qi, which is empty and simply waits for things (chapter 4). An anxious mind tries to foresee everything so as not to miss anything, and Taoism looks at this with gentle sympathy. Zhuangzi described how people, day and night, grapple with everything they meet, wearing out their hearts with small and large worries — and how this wears life away. The Taoist answer isn’t even more control, but wu wei, non-action: not doing nothing, but letting go of needless, forceful effort. Water doesn’t plan its path in advance, yet it always finds its way. Such a heart is like an empty room that light comes into. You can accept anxiety as a wave — and let it pass through without clinging.
anxiety.practice: For a minute, listen to the sounds around you without naming them — “not with the ears but with the breath,” as in the fasting of the heart. Imagine that your heart is an empty, bright room that anxiety passes right through.

fear.text: At a waterfall where the water dropped thirty ren, Confucius saw a swimmer in the churning current and sent his disciples to rescue him — but the man climbed out on his own and walked off singing (Zhuangzi, chapter 19). The Taoists didn’t consider fear a disgrace. But they noticed that fear often arises when we hold on to one side of life and dread the other: we cling to success and fear failure, cling to health and fear illness. The Tao Te Ching says that opposites give birth to each other: difficult and easy, long and short, high and low. For a Taoist, the world is constant transformation, and every change holds not only a threat but a possibility. Later the swimmer explained: he went down with the whirlpool and came up with it, never setting himself against the water. You can meet fear the same way — not freezing in resistance, but moving along with what is happening, step by step.
fear.practice: Stand up and rock gently from heels to toes, like a swimmer on a wave — not resisting, but following. Then ask yourself: what would one step “with the current” look like?

sadness.text: The character yin originally meant the shady slope of a hill, and yang the sunny one: not good and evil, but two sides of the same hill. Sadness is as natural as autumn or dusk, and Taoism sees no reason to be ashamed of it. In the Taoist picture of the world everything moves in cycles: a rise is followed by a fall, light by shadow, yang passes into yin so as to become yang again. Sadness is a yin time: quiet, slow, turned inward. The Tao Te Ching says that turning back into its opposite is the movement of the Tao, and softness and weakness are how it works. Sadness isn’t a malfunction but one of the natural rhythms, like an ebb tide. A Taoist would say that there’s no need to force yourself into cheerfulness; you can let this time be. Just as winter doesn’t hinder spring but prepares for it, sadness can turn out to be a time of quietly gathering strength within.
sadness.practice: Picture which slope of the hill you are on right now — shady or sunny — and what someone sitting in the shade needs: rest, warmth, quiet? Give yourself a little of it.

grief.text: When Zhuangzi’s wife died, his friend Huizi came to offer condolences and found him sitting on the ground, drumming on a basin and singing. Loss is a great pain, and Taoism doesn’t deny it. To his indignant friend Zhuangzi replied that at first, of course, he had grieved like anyone. But then he reflected: once she had not existed; then out of a dim chaos came breath, qi; from it a form; from the form, life; now another transformation had taken place, like the passing of spring, summer, autumn and winter. This story doesn’t suggest you stop grieving — Zhuangzi himself grieved. It shows that in time the pain can join with a sense of the great cycle of which the loved one was a part. You can grieve and at the same time feel that your bond with them has not vanished from the world.
grief.practice: Go out to a tree or the open sky and silently tell the one you lost: “I remember you.” Listen to the wind — Zhuangzi would say it too is part of the same great cycle.

loneliness.text: In the first chapter of the Zhuangzi, the enormous fish Kun turns into the bird Peng, whose back is like Mount Tai and whose wings are like clouds covering half the sky. Loneliness is painful, and longing for closeness is natural. Taoism, though, also sees a bright side to solitude. Zhuangzi wrote of “free and easy wandering” — a state in which the spirit isn’t tied to others’ approval and can soar far and wide, like the enormous bird Peng in his parable. Taoist hermits went off into the mountains not out of resentment toward people, but to hear the silence and feel their connection with “the ten thousand things” — the Chinese name for all the multiplicity of the world. Taoism would say you are never completely cut off: you are part of the same nature as the trees, the wind, other people. Loneliness can become a time when this connection is felt more quietly, but more deeply. And longing for people is also a natural movement you can follow.
loneliness.practice: Call one person today just because, with no errand — like a stream that finds another stream by itself. If there’s no one to call, say a few warm words to a neighbor or a shopkeeper.

anger.text: A young tree bends in the wind and straightens again, while a dry one snaps — Laozi saw in this the whole secret of strength (chapter 76). Anger is a powerful energy, and there’s nothing unnatural about it. Taoism, however, pays attention to how it works. The Tao Te Ching keeps returning to the image of water: it is the softest thing in the world, yet it wears away the hardest stone. Strength, for Laozi, lies not in rigidity but in flexibility: what is hard and unbending is closer to death, and what is soft and supple is closer to life, like a young tree that bends in the wind but doesn’t break. Laozi might say that anger frozen into rigid opposition exhausts you first of all. But its energy can be directed differently — like water, which doesn’t argue with a stone but flows around it and still reaches its goal. You can admit “I’m angry” — and choose a path that is gentle but persistent.
anger.practice: Unclench your jaw, drop your shoulders and take three breaths out, like water flowing around a stone. Then ask: what gentle but persistent step would bring me closer to what I actually want?

quote.text: In the world there is nothing more submissive and weak than water. Yet for attacking that which is hard and strong nothing can surpass it.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 78 (trans. D. C. Lau)

shame.text: Carpenter Shi walked past an enormous oak without even a glance: “A useless tree.” That night the oak appeared to him in a dream and asked, “What are you comparing me with?” (chapter 4). Shame is often born of measuring yourself against standards: how you ought to be, what is proper, what counts as success. Taoism treats such standards with deep distrust. Laozi wrote that when everyone recognizes beauty as beautiful, ugliness appears: judgments give birth to their doubles. Zhuangzi collected stories of people with disabilities, strange looks or low standing who were wise and drew others to them. The oak explained to the carpenter that its very “uselessness” had saved it from the axe, and so it grew enormous. For a Taoist, what embarrasses you may turn out to be part of your true nature — pu, “the uncarved block,” a simplicity that doesn’t need to be trimmed to fit someone else’s pattern.
shame.practice: Say out loud the standard by which you are shaming yourself, then ask, like the oak in the carpenter’s dream: “What are you comparing me with?” Whose standard is it — yours or someone else’s?

guilt.text: Why did the ancients prize the Tao so highly? Laozi asks in chapter 62, and answers: because, having found it, the guilty are freed from their guilt. Guilt tells you that the consequences of your actions matter to you, and that’s important. Taoism says little about guilt in our usual sense — it is more interested in naturalness than in moral rules. Laozi even remarked that loud talk of benevolence and righteousness appears when the great Way has been lost — living, spontaneous kindness. A Taoist would say that guilt is useful as long as it brings you back to that simple kindness, and harmful when it turns into endless self-condemnation. The Tao Te Ching asks: who can, by being still, make muddy water clear? Water that is no longer stirred clears by itself. You can admit your mistake, set right what is possible, and let the muddy water settle.
guilt.practice: Set right one thing that can be set right — apologize, give back, help. Then stir a pinch of tea leaves into a glass of water and watch for a minute as the cloudiness settles by itself.

envy.text: The one-legged beast Kui envied the millipede, the millipede envied the snake, the snake the wind, the wind the eye, and the eye the heart — so begins one of the parables of the Zhuangzi (chapter 17). Envy is a natural echo of comparison, and you don’t need to be ashamed of it. Taoism, however, looks at comparison itself with suspicion. The Tao Te Ching says there is no greater misfortune than not knowing when enough is enough, and that one who knows contentment is always content. This isn’t about resigning yourself to want, but about inner freedom: as long as your happiness is measured by other people’s successes, it is always in their hands. Each has its own makeup and its own path. Laozi might say that you can take envy as a reminder to return to your own nature — and to what you already have.
envy.practice: Like the one-legged Kui, walk for a few minutes at your own pace — no faster and no slower than feels right. On the way, name one thing that exists only on your path.

quote.text: There is no disaster greater than not being content; there is no misfortune greater than being covetous. Hence in being content, one will always have enough.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 46 (trans. D. C. Lau)

emptiness.text: Huizi grew an enormous gourd, but it was too big for a jug and too flat for a ladle, so he smashed it. “Why not make it into a boat and float along the rivers and lakes?” Zhuangzi wondered. Emptiness and apathy can be heavy, and they deserve gentle care. Taoism can offer an unexpected view: in its language, emptiness is not only a lack but also a source of possibility. Laozi gives examples: a wheel works thanks to the emptiness at its hub, a jug thanks to the emptiness inside, a room thanks to the openings of its windows and doors. Usefulness arises where there is space. For a Taoist, your present emptiness isn’t necessarily an ending, but perhaps a cleared space in which something new hasn’t appeared yet. There’s no need to fill it in a hurry. The Taoists spoke of xu — the emptiness, the openness of the heart in which calm is born. You can simply stay in this state, looking after your body and your rest, and let the new come in its own time.
emptiness.practice: Look at any vessel nearby — a cup, a bowl — and notice: it is useful thanks to its emptiness. Ask yourself: what might space be clearing in me for?

quote.text: Thirty spokes share one hub. Adapt the nothing therein to the purpose in hand, and you will have the use of the cart.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 11 (trans. D. C. Lau)

confusion.text: “Everyone else is clear and bright; I alone am murky. Everyone else is discerning; I alone am dim, like a wave on the sea,” Laozi writes of himself in chapter 20. Confusion is an honest state, when the old answers no longer fit, and Taoism, strange as it may seem, values this “not-knowing.” The opening lines of the Tao Te Ching say that what matters most doesn’t fit into ready-made formulas. Zhuangzi told how he once dreamed he was a butterfly, fluttering about carefree — and on waking he couldn’t tell whether it was Zhuangzi who had dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming it was Zhuangzi. This parable teaches lightness toward uncertainty. A Taoist would say that you don’t have to understand everything right away. You can move like water: without knowing the whole map, but sensing the nearest slope of the ground. Clarity often comes by itself once you stop hurrying it.
confusion.practice: Go for a walk with no route, and at each corner turn wherever it’s easiest to go. Notice how your feet choose the way — and ask which next step in your situation runs “downhill.”

quote.text: The way that can be spoken of is not the constant way.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 1 (trans. D. C. Lau)

fatigue.text: Cook Ding carved up an ox so that his movements looked like a dance, and in nineteen years his knife never once grew dull (chapter 3). Tiredness and burnout are a sign that you’ve been going against your own current for a long time. Taoism understands this very well. The cook’s secret was that he didn’t hack at random, but followed the natural gaps and joints, finding the path of least resistance. Ordinary cooks change their knife every month, because they hack at bone. Laozi might say that burnout is when we have been “hacking at bone” for too long: spending our strength on struggle rather than on moving along natural lines. Wu wei, non-action, isn’t laziness but the art of acting without needless force against yourself. Rest and a return to your own rhythm are part of the Way too.
fatigue.practice: Stretch slowly, like a cat looking for a comfortable position — not by force, but along the “natural joints” of your body. Where the movement comes easily, linger there.

boredom.text: “Look how freely the little fish swim — that is the joy of fish,” Zhuangzi said as he strolled with Huizi on the bridge over the Hao River. “You’re not a fish — how do you know?” his friend objected (chapter 17). Boredom can be oppressive: the world seems flat and time empty, and it often comes from expecting life to entertain us with something special. The argument was philosophical, but the scene itself shows the Taoist attention to the simple: to fish, water, the moment. For a Taoist, the ordinary holds inexhaustible variety — “the ten thousand things,” constantly changing. You can accept boredom as a pause in which the eye learns to see anew, without hurry.
boredom.practice: Choose one ordinary thing nearby — a leaf, a cloud, the steam over a cup — and watch it for a minute, the way Zhuangzi watched the fish.

joy.text: Zhuangzi filled his book with talking trees, arguing frogs and turtles, wise cripples and chattering winds — it is perhaps the most cheerful book of antiquity. Joy is a natural expression of life, and Taoism welcomes it, especially when it is simple and unforced. The book’s first chapter is called “Free and Easy Wandering” — about the lightness of a spirit not bound by rules or by concern for gain. In the Taoist sense, joy is especially pure when it is ziran — “so of itself,” natural, not squeezed out of yourself and not dependent on anyone’s approval. At the same time, the Taoists remembered that everything turns into its opposite, and they didn’t try to hold on to joy forever. That is exactly why you can live it fully: like a wind that comes and goes, leaving freshness behind.
joy.practice: Do something today just for the sake of it, with no use at all: whistle, swing on a swing, wander without a goal. Zhuangzi would call it a small free and easy wandering.

love.text: “I have three treasures,” says Laozi, “the first of them is love; from love, courage is born” (chapter 67). Love and tenderness are among the most natural feelings, and in Taoism they are close to the very nature of the Way. In the original the word is ci, translated as love, compassion or motherly care. In the Tao Te Ching the Tao is often described in motherly images — as the mother of all under heaven, who gives birth to and nourishes everything while possessing nothing. For a Taoist, the deepest love is like this: it gives life without claiming, cares without controlling. You can take the tenderness you feel as an expression of this natural power — soft, but very strong.
love.practice: Offer someone close one act of care “the Taoist way” — light and without expectations: make them tea, leave a warm note, asking nothing in return.

gratitude.text: The Tao, for Laozi, gives birth to and nourishes all things — it “gives life but does not possess, acts but does not ask for gratitude” (chapter 51). Gratitude is a warm feeling of connection with what sustains your life. Taoist texts say little about gratitude as a moral duty, but it probably grows naturally out of seeing the Tao. Gratitude in this sense isn’t a reckoning of who owes whom, but wonder at the world’s generosity: air, water, light, the people nearby. Laozi wrote that one who knows contentment is rich. Gratitude helps you accept life as it is, noticing that even on hard days much goes on giving itself unconditionally.
gratitude.practice: Step outside for a minute and whisper thanks to three things that asked nothing in return today: the air, the light, someone’s smile.

hope.text: An old man living right at the frontier lost his horse. “How do you know this isn’t for the good?” he asked his sympathetic neighbors (Huainanzi). Hope helps us get through hard times, and Taoism gives it a special kind of support — not a promise that everything will be fine, but an understanding of how change works. The Tao Te Ching says that misfortune and good fortune are intertwined and pass into one another. The horse came back, bringing a fine stallion with it, and the story kept turning first one way, then the other. A Taoist would say that your present situation isn’t a final verdict. Hope here isn’t clinging to a particular outcome but openness: everything flows, and every situation already holds the seeds of something new.
hope.practice: Ask yourself the frontier old man’s question — “Who knows whether this is for the good?” — about your present situation. Then recall one failure from the past that later turned into something important.

quote.text: It is on disaster that good fortune perches; it is beneath good fortune that disaster crouches.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 58 (trans. D. C. Lau)

nostalgia.text: Laozi advised “returning to the state of the infant” and to “the uncarved block” — to the simplicity that existed before all the add-ons (chapter 28). Nostalgia is a tender longing for what has gone, and it reflects what is truly dear to you. Taoism sees this feeling as a natural response to the world’s main law — constant transformation. Zhuangzi spoke of ceaseless change, in which things pass into one another, and taught us to meet it without reproach. Laozi wrote of “returning to the root”: all the multiplicity of life ultimately returns to its source, and he called this return stillness. Laozi might say that nostalgia is a longing for the root, for that state of simplicity and wholeness we once felt. To touch it, you don’t have to bring back the past: the root is always here, in the quiet and simplicity of the present moment.
nostalgia.practice: Do one thing today “from that time” in your present circumstances: cook that same porridge, play that song, walk somewhere the way you used to. Let the root sprout here.

craving.text: An old Chinese book, the Caigentan, has an image: the wind passes through sparse bamboo, and once it has gone, it leaves no sound behind. A craving — a sharp “I want it now” — can be as powerful as a current, and there’s no need to be ashamed of it. The Taoists didn’t condemn desires, but they looked closely at how they work. Laozi noticed that chasing ever stronger sensations doesn’t satisfy but dulls the senses: the more insistently we chase a stimulus, the less it gives. He saw the way out not in struggle but in pu — simplicity, the image of the uncarved block, the natural state before all the add-ons. The Taoist approach to a wave of craving is wu wei, non-action: neither rushing into battle nor giving in, but letting the wave rise and pass, the way wind passes through bamboo. In the Taoist picture, everything that reaches its limit turns back — and so does a craving.
craving.practice: When the craving comes, stand like bamboo: feet steady, body soft. Sway slightly with each exhale and wait for the “wind” to pass through you — usually it takes a few minutes.

addiction.text: A tree as thick as your arms can reach grows from a tiny sprout; a nine-story tower begins with a handful of earth, Laozi wrote (chapter 64). Addiction isn’t a moral failure, but a deep rut that life slides back into again and again. The Taoists spoke a great deal about how life’s natural movement can freeze. Zhuangzi told of Cook Ding, who carved an ox so easily that his knife stayed sharp for nineteen years: he didn’t hack his way through but found the natural gaps between the joints. One thought can be drawn from this image: the way out of the circle is rarely found through force and a sudden lunge — more often through a patient search for “gaps,” places where you can pass more gently. Laozi valued water, which slowly but steadily changes stone. Taoism also speaks of “returning to the root” — to the simple and natural. This is a path of small steps, and every one of them counts.
addiction.practice: Tell someone who understands — a friend, or a mutual-help group — about your “gap,” a moment when the circle loosens even a little. It is a handful of earth for a new tower.

hangover.text: “Reach the limit of emptiness, hold fast to stillness,” Laozi advised: everything grows and clamors, and then returns to its root (chapter 16). The morning after — a heavy body, anxiety, shame, fragments of yesterday — deserves gentleness, not a verdict. The Taoists saw life as an alternation of yin and yang: a rise is followed by a fall, noise by quiet, excess by depletion. A hard morning is a pendulum swinging back, not proof of your worthlessness. Taoist wisdom here is not to put yourself on trial, but to return to the simple: quiet, rest, slow breathing. Laozi called this “returning to the root.” Going over yesterday can wait until your head is clearer — then you’ll see what really needs attention and what was only morning anxiety.
hangover.practice: Allow yourself a few minutes of not deciding anything about yesterday. Just sit, feeling the support beneath you and your slow breathing.

euphoria.text: Whoever stands on tiptoe won’t stand for long; whoever takes strides too wide won’t get far, Laozi observed (chapter 24). A burst of euphoria is bright, and you can live it with joy. Taoism isn’t against highs: Zhuangzi is one of the most cheerful philosophers, and his “free and easy wandering” is full of lightness. But the Taoists saw that everything in the world moves in a circle: having reached its peak, any phenomenon begins to turn back. The Tao Te Ching says that returning, turning into the opposite, is the very movement of the Tao. Knowing this doesn’t spoil the high but makes it lighter: there’s no need to cling and try to hold on to the peak. The Taoist sage never flies higher than they can calmly come down from. Enjoying the wave while remembering the shore — that is Taoist grace.
euphoria.practice: Stand on your whole foot — not on tiptoe — and do something small and earthy: drink some tea, take a walk. Let the joy be — and let it have something to stand on.

crash.text: The moon, once full, begins to wane, and the sun, having reached its zenith, leans toward sunset — the Taoists took this old Chinese thought as the law of all things. The drop after a high can be disheartening: yesterday everything shone, today it’s gray. Taoism sees this not as a breakdown but as a natural rhythm. Yin and yang pass into each other like day and night, and the drop is as much a part of the cycle as the rise. Laozi wrote that what is hollow becomes full, and what is worn becomes new. After yang — bright, loud, active — comes yin: quiet, rest, recovery. If you don’t wage war on the drop, it becomes a time when strength gathers anew, like the earth in winter. The Taoist advice is not to drive yourself back up to the peak, but to let yourself stay in the lowland for a while. Water, Laozi reminds us, flows downward — and that is exactly why it is closest to the Tao.
crash.practice: Make today a “yin day”: choose one quiet, restoring activity and allow it to yourself without guilt.

panic.text: The true person, Zhuangzi wrote, breathes from their very heels, while ordinary people breathe from the throat (chapter 6). A wave of panic is truly frightening: your heart pounds, you can’t get enough air — and it isn’t your fault that it came. The Tao Te Ching has a simple observation about the nature of storms: even heaven and earth can’t keep up a gale or a downpour for long. The wave inside a person is weather too: it rises and recedes. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. The Taoist image here is wu wei: not fighting the wave with all your might, since struggle often spurs it on, but becoming like water, which rides out a storm without breaking. You can hold on to something simple and steady while the wave passes.
panic.practice: Press your heels into the floor and imagine that each in-breath starts from them, as Zhuangzi taught. Make the exhale longer than the inhale and silently name five things you can see around you.

quote.text: A gusty wind cannot last all morning, and a sudden downpour cannot last all day.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 23 (trans. D. C. Lau)

dread.text: When Zhuangzi was dying, his disciples wanted to give him a lavish funeral, and he replied: heaven and earth will be my coffin, the sun and moon my jade, the stars my pearls (chapter 32). The thought of our finitude and the question “what’s the point of it all” are very ancient experiences. The Taoists looked into the same abyss, but saw in it not emptiness but a great movement. Zhuangzi described the world as a ceaseless “transformation of things”: everything arises from the Tao and returns to it, like the seasons. He also insisted that our small mind cannot grasp the whole — and that this is not a tragedy but a relief: you don’t need to know the answer to “what is it all for” in order to live. Meaning in Taoism isn’t a goal somewhere ahead, but the very flow of life: breath, the turning of the seasons, a conversation with a friend. Instead of the question of meaning, you can for a while trust the movement you are part of.
dread.practice: Go to the window or step outside, and for a minute watch something moving — clouds, leaves, people. Feel that you are part of this movement.

fomo.text: A cicada and a little dove laughed at the enormous bird Peng: why fly ninety thousand li, when it’s enough for us to reach the nearest elm? When it seems everyone else lives more interesting lives and you’re not where you should be, it wears you out — especially in the age of the feed, where other people’s lives are on display around the clock. Zhuangzi shows that each has its own scale and its own measure. Someone else’s life, seen in the feed, is no yardstick for yours. Laozi wrote that one who knows contentment is rich — meaning the ability to feel: this is enough for me. The Taoist sage doesn’t run off to where “the important things are happening”: the important things happen wherever the sage is.
fomo.practice: Ask yourself, like the cicada in Zhuangzi: “Which flight is mine?” Name one thing in today that is truly enough for you.

sleepless.text: The true person of old, Zhuangzi wrote, slept without dreams and woke without worries (chapter 6). Thoughts at three in the morning circle like leaves in a whirlpool, and they are hard to shake off. The Taoists would say that night is a yin time, a time of rest and darkness, while the mind sometimes goes on living in the day, in yang: deciding, arguing, planning. Laozi asked: who can make muddy water clear? — and answered: if you leave it still, it will gradually clear. Night thoughts are the same muddy water: the more you stir it, the less you can see. The Taoist way is wu wei: not forcing yourself to fall asleep, but ceasing to struggle, letting thoughts drift past like clouds. Sleep, like everything natural, comes when it isn’t dragged.
sleepless.practice: Lying down, imagine that your thoughts are muddy water in a bowl. Don’t touch it; just watch the silt slowly settle to the bottom.

betrayal.text: Zhuangzi lived in the Warring States period, when yesterday’s allies became enemies overnight and advisers were brought down by their friends’ denunciations. Betrayal wounds where there was trust, and your pain is entirely natural. The Taoists saw plenty of human faithlessness. Their answer is neither to harden nor to pretend nothing happened. Laozi observed that what is alive is soft and supple, while what has withered is hard and brittle, and so he saw rigidity as the companion of decline and softness as the companion of life. Protecting yourself and keeping your distance is natural. But you don’t have to let betrayal turn your heart to stone. Laozi might say that in time the wound can become a place where you understand people better, rather than a place of permanent defense.
betrayal.practice: Notice where in your body you are holding this pain — your shoulders, your jaw? Let that place soften, even for a few breaths.

jealousy.text: Liezi tells of a man who lost his axe and suspected his neighbor’s son: the boy walked like a thief, looked like a thief, talked like a thief; and when the axe turned up, the neighbor’s son looked like an ordinary person again. Jealousy is a mix of love, fear and insecurity, and there’s nothing shameful in it. For a Taoist, jealousy is an attempt to hold on to something that is by nature alive and free. Laozi wrote of the Tao that gives birth but does not claim, that nurtures but does not possess. Love in the Taoist spirit is like this: it nourishes but doesn’t hold by force. This doesn’t mean you should stay silent about your feelings. But you can notice where fear makes you clench your fist — and try to loosen it a little, leaning on your own inner steadiness.
jealousy.practice: Recall the parable of the axe and ask yourself: what do I know for certain in this situation, and what have I “drawn in,” like that man with his neighbor’s walk? Name one need you could speak about honestly.

resentment.text: If an empty boat drifts into your boat on the river, you won’t get angry, even if you’re hot-tempered; but if someone is sitting in it, you’ll start shouting (Zhuangzi, chapter 20). An old grudge is heavy, and it usually grew out of a real injustice. Taoism doesn’t demand that you forget it, but it notices how it keeps a person in the past. Zhuangzi doesn’t claim the one who hurt you is blameless. He invites you to see that a good part of the torment lies in the image of the other person that we carry with us for years. The Taoist way is to “empty your boat,” not to keep the old cargo on board. Letting go of a grudge doesn’t mean excusing it; it means freeing your own current.
resentment.practice: Picture your boat, and the grudge as a heavy sack on board. With each exhale, lower one part of it into the water in your mind — not all at once — and notice how the boat gradually rises.

heartbreak.text: Fish stranded on dry land moisten each other with their breath and wet each other with foam — but better for them to forget each other in the rivers and lakes (Zhuangzi, chapter 6). A breakup is a huge change, and the pain of a broken heart is entirely real. The Taoists saw life as a flow in which meetings and partings follow one another like the seasons. This doesn’t make the pain smaller, but it helps you not take it as proof that something is wrong with you. Laozi wrote that difficult and easy, high and low give rise to each other. The depth of your sadness is the other side of the depth of your love. The Taoist way is not to hurry yourself or force the feeling: winter doesn’t turn into spring on command. But spring does come. While the yin time lasts, you can care for yourself gently, the way a gardener cares for sleeping earth.
heartbreak.practice: Ask yourself: “What care do I need in this ‘winter’?” Choose one gentle thing and do it for yourself today.

impostor.text: Wheelwright Bian, shaping a wheel below the terrace, asked the duke what he was reading. “The words of the sages.” “Then it’s the leftovers of the ancients,” said the wheelwright: he felt his own skill in his hands and couldn’t pass it on in words even to his son (chapter 13). The fear of being “found out” often comes to people who are actually trying hard and growing. Taoism looks at it in an unusual way: Laozi didn’t trust loud claims to knowledge at all. The sage in the Taoist picture is modest, senses the limits of their understanding and isn’t ashamed of them. Your feeling of “I don’t know everything” isn’t evidence against you but a sign of honesty. Real skill lives in practice, not in titles and speeches. You’re not an impostor if you are learning your craft by doing it.
impostor.practice: Do one thing with your hands that you know how to do — slice bread, sew on a button, fix a line of code — and notice how this knowledge lives in your fingers, not in words.

quote.text: One who knows does not speak; one who speaks does not know.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 56 (trans. D. C. Lau)

self_hatred.text: Ai Taituo was so ugly he frightened the whole realm — and yet people were drawn to him, and the Duke of Lu wanted to entrust him with the state (Zhuangzi, chapter 5). If your inner critic is loud and merciless right now, you deserve gentleness, not agreement with its verdict. Taoism is especially far from self-flagellation. Zhuangzi loved “useless” characters: the crooked, gnarled tree that a carpenter judged worthless — and which, precisely for that reason, grew enormous and gave shade to many. He told of people with disabilities who were laughed at, yet in whom there was a remarkable fullness of de, inner power. The yardsticks your critic judges you by are often other people’s measures of “usefulness” and “correctness.” The Taoist thought is this: you don’t have to live up to them. Like a tree, you grow in your own shape.
self_hatred.practice: Say to your critic out loud: “A crooked tree gives shade too.” Then name one quality it calls a flaw, and ask where strength might be hiding in it.

helplessness.text: The Foolish Old Man set out to level the two mountains by his house — basket by basket — and answered those who mocked him: after me come my children and grandchildren, and the mountains won’t grow any taller (Liezi). Feeling powerless to change something is agonizing, and it’s important not to blame yourself for it. Laozi wrote that the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong, and that water, the most yielding thing in the world, wears away stone. This isn’t a consoling fairy tale: water doesn’t break a rock in a day; it acts constantly, little by little, finding the cracks. For a Taoist, helplessness before something large doesn’t cancel your “power of water” — a small but persistent presence. Wu wei isn’t passivity but action in harmony with circumstances: not beating your head against the wall, but looking for where it gives. And sometimes the best you can do is simply hold steady, like bamboo in the wind.
helplessness.practice: Carry one “basket of earth” today — one gentle, almost unnoticeable action toward what seems immovable.

procrastination.text: Laozi advised tackling the difficult while it is easy, and the great while it is small (chapter 63). When you just can’t get started, it doesn’t make you a lazy person. Taoism invites you to look at this state without forcing yourself. Laozi wrote that great things are made from small ones, and that the difficult begins with the easy. Often a task seems like a huge mountain, and the mind freezes before it. The Taoist move isn’t to storm the mountain, but to find the easiest place for the first step. Wu wei here isn’t idleness but the search for a beginning that doesn’t require breaking yourself. Water doesn’t argue with stone: it simply flows where the way is open. In the same way, a task begun with something small gradually gathers its current.
procrastination.practice: Find the easiest little piece of the task — so small it’s almost embarrassing to call it work. Do only that.

quote.text: The journey of a thousand miles starts from beneath one’s feet.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 64 (trans. D. C. Lau)

uprooted.text: Legend has it that in his old age Laozi mounted a black ox and rode west, and the keeper of the frontier pass begged him to write down his teaching before he left — and so a book of five thousand characters came to be. Losing your home — a move, emigration — knocks the ground out from under your feet, and longing for what came before is entirely natural. The Taoist tradition knows about wandering. The first chapter of the Zhuangzi is called “Free and Easy Wandering” — about a person who finds support not in a place but in harmony with the Tao. The “root” Laozi speaks of isn’t only the land where you were born, but also a quiet center within, which you can return to anywhere. This doesn’t cancel the loss. But you aren’t an uprooted plant — you’re more like a seed looking for new soil, carrying everything that is yours within it.
uprooted.practice: Find one natural thing in your new place — a tree, a river, the sky above the rooftops — and spend a minute with it. It is the same as everywhere.

overload.text: The sage, according to Laozi, cares for the belly and not for the eyes (chapter 12). When the feed, notifications and noise never end, the mind grows tired, and that is natural. Laozi described something similar two and a half thousand years ago, long before any screens: an excess of impressions doesn’t enrich the senses but dulls them. Caring for the belly means caring for what truly nourishes rather than what merely catches the eye. The Taoist answer to overload is pu, simplicity. Taoist hygiene of the mind means returning from time to time to a few things: one sound, one taste, one task — and letting the rest go by.
overload.practice: Choose one simple sensation — the taste of tea, a sound outside the window — and stay with it alone for a minute, with the screen set aside.

quote.text: The five colours make man’s eyes blind; the five notes make his ears deaf; the five tastes injure his palate.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 12 (trans. D. C. Lau)

unreality.text: Once Zhuang Zhou dreamed he was a butterfly, fluttering about carefree; on waking, he couldn’t tell whether Zhou had dreamed he was a butterfly, or a butterfly was dreaming it was Zhou (chapter 2). When the world or you yourself seem unreal, as if in a dream, it’s a strange, sometimes unsettling experience, and it can be talked about calmly. Remarkably, this story isn’t frightening but light: Zhuangzi ends it with the thought of “the transformation of things.” Sleep and waking, butterfly and man are forms of one continuous flow. Taoism doesn’t demand that you urgently settle what is “real.” And you can find support in the simple: here is your breath, here is the ground under your feet.
unreality.practice: Touch something with a pronounced texture — wood, fabric, stone — and describe the sensation to yourself. Let this touch be your bridge back to “here.”

awe.text: In autumn, when the rivers flooded, He Bo, the spirit of the Yellow River, grew proud of his breadth — until he reached the Northern Sea and saw that it had no shores (chapter 17). Awe before something vast or beautiful — mountains, the sky, the sea — is one of the most living experiences. Taoism, arguably, grew largely out of this feeling. The Tao, for Laozi, cannot be expressed in words; it is greater than any name, and it is natural to fall silent before it. Awe is a moment when you, like that river, suddenly see the scale of the world. In the Taoist sense this isn’t a humiliation but the joy of belonging to the whole. Such a feeling doesn’t need explaining — it’s enough to stay in it for a while.
awe.practice: When you feel awe, stay silent for a minute, naming nothing. Just let yourself be a small part of something immense.

relief.text: Laozi compared the way of heaven to the stringing of a bow: what is raised too high is lowered, and what is low is raised (chapter 77). The long-awaited breath out of relief can simply be lived. Taoism sees in it the natural swing of a pendulum: tension has given way to release, yang to yin. Relief shows how much strength was going into holding the tension. The Taoist advice is not to rush straight on to the next worry, but to let body and mind stay in the released state, the way a slackened bowstring rests. The wisdom of the Tao lies in alternation, not in endless effort. In the Taoist picture, rest isn’t a reward to be earned but just as legitimate a part of the cycle as work. Now is the time to let go.
relief.practice: Take a long breath out and let your shoulders go, like a slackened bowstring. Stay in this “released” state for a few breaths, without hurrying to the next thing.

calm.text: People look at their reflection not in running water but in still water, Zhuangzi observed: only a calm surface reflects clearly (chapter 5). Calm is a precious state, and for Taoism it is almost a homecoming. Laozi wrote: returning to the root is called stillness. Everything grows, blossoms, rustles — and then returns to its source, to silence. Taoist calm isn’t freezing up, but a depth like still water. Your calm makes you such a mirror — in it the world can be seen more distinctly. There’s no need to hold on to it by force: it’s enough to learn the way to it, so you can return again. The Taoists believed calm isn’t a rare gift but a natural state that everything tends to return to by itself, if only we stop getting in the way.
calm.practice: Stay in your calm for a minute, imagining yourself as still water. Notice what is reflected in it — which sounds, images, sensations.

inspiration.text: Woodworker Qing made a bell stand so beautiful that people took it for the work of spirits; he explained that he had fasted for seven days until he forgot rewards, praise and even his own body — and only then went into the forest (chapter 19). Inspiration is a living surge when you want to create, and Taoism values this state highly. Zhuangzi loved such craftsmen: they worked as if not by their own will but in harmony with the nature of things. In the forest Qing saw a tree in which the finished form was already hidden. Taoist inspiration isn’t strained effort but ziran, naturalness: you stop getting in the way of what wants to be born. A Taoist’s advice to someone inspired is to follow this current, without hurrying to claim the result as your own.
inspiration.practice: Before you take up your idea, set aside thoughts of results and evaluations for a minute. Ask yourself, like Woodworker Qing: “What shape does this want to take?”

schadenfreude.text: Zhuangzi was walking through a chestnut grove and saw a cicada in the shade; a mantis was creeping up on it, a magpie on the mantis, and he himself was already aiming at the magpie — when the keeper chased him off as a thief (chapter 20). Schadenfreude is something people hide even from themselves, though almost everyone has felt it. Taoism would look at it through one of its favorite ideas — the relativity of good and bad fortune. The Huainanzi has a parable about an old man on the frontier whose horse ran away. The neighbors commiserated, but he asked: “How do you know this isn’t good luck?” The horse came back with a herd; then his son fell from a horse and was lamed; then, because of the limp, he wasn’t taken off to war. Laozi might say that someone else’s failure is just one turn in the long alternation of yin and yang, and rejoicing in it is as premature as grieving over your own. You can notice schadenfreude as a sign that you’re measuring yourself against others — and gently return to your own current.
schadenfreude.practice: When you feel schadenfreude, recall the chestnut grove and look around: who might be watching me the same way right now? Then turn your attention to your own affairs.

contempt.text: People consider Mao Qiang and Xi Shi beauties, but fish, on seeing them, dive into the depths, and birds fly high into the sky — so who knows true beauty? (Zhuangzi, chapter 2). Contempt divides the world into high and low — and Taoism treats such divisions with deep distrust. With this example, in the chapter “On the Equality of Things,” Zhuangzi shows that everyone judges from their own standpoint. For a Taoist, contempt is a frozen judgment that mistakes a particular view for the final one. Laozi advised us to “blunt our sharpness” (chapter 56). This doesn’t mean approving of everything. But you can notice: what you despise is seen from a particular place, and from another place the world looks different. Contempt grows lighter when you step down from the pedestal.
contempt.practice: For a minute, try looking at the situation through the eyes of the person you feel contempt for: how does the world look from where they stand? You don’t have to agree — just look.

quote.text: He who knows others is clever; he who knows himself has discernment. He who overcomes others has force; he who overcomes himself is strong.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 33 (trans. D. C. Lau)

disgust.text: “Where is the Tao?” Zhuangzi was asked. “Everywhere.” “Be more specific.” “In the ant.” “And lower still?” “In the weeds, in a potsherd, in piss and dung.” The questioner fell silent (chapter 22). Disgust is one of the strongest responses of recoil, and it can be directed at people, situations and yourself. Taoism pays special attention to what we consider low and dirty. A Taoist would say that the Way disdains nothing, and the division into clean and dirty is a human judgment. This doesn’t mean disgust is wrong: it protects. But it can soften if you remember that both what repels you and you yourself are part of one cycle. If the disgust is turned on yourself, Taoism would remind you: the Way doesn’t turn away from you either.
disgust.practice: Name what disgusts you and add: “And this, too, is part of the world.” Notice whether anything in your body shifts — even slightly.

revenge.text: Laozi advised answering injury with virtue, and noted that after a great enmity some resentment always remains — so how can that be called good? (chapters 63 and 79). You were hurt, and you want to restore the balance — the wish to pay back is natural for someone wounded. Taoism speaks of balance too, but understands it differently. This isn’t naivety: for a Taoist, revenge is an attempt to bend the course of things by force, and violence breeds answering violence, spreading in circles like ripples on water. The image of water suggests something else too: water doesn’t take revenge on a stone, but flows around it and continues on its way. Laozi might say that the strongest thing you can do with a hurt is not to let it define your path. You need your energy for your own current, not for punishing someone else.
revenge.practice: Picture your hurt as a stone in a river and for a minute watch the water flow around it on both sides. Then name out loud one step of yours that flows on instead of beating against the stone.

anger_at_loved.text: “Don’t be like the mantis that angrily raises its forelegs against a chariot wheel,” Zhuangzi advised someone who had to live alongside a difficult person (chapter 4). Anger at those close to you — a partner, parents, children — is especially painful, because shame quickly follows it. Taoism invites you to look at this through yin and yang: in every living bond there is attraction and repulsion, warmth and irritation, and one never comes without the other. The closer the person, the more often your currents collide. For a Taoist, anger often concerns not the person themselves but the collision, and it doesn’t have to be turned into a war. An outburst is like a gust of wind that doesn’t last all day. Afterward you can return to gentleness, without punishing yourself.
anger_at_loved.practice: After an outburst, take three slow breaths out and say to your loved one one short sentence without reproach: “I snapped; it was hard for me.” The rest can wait.

ambivalence.text: In the yin-yang symbol there is always a dark dot in the light half and a light dot in the dark one, and they flow into each other ceaselessly. Loving someone and at the same time being unable to stand them — it seems it shouldn’t be this way, but for Taoism it is entirely natural. Laozi wrote that opposites give birth to one another: difficult and easy complete each other, long and short define each other (chapter 2). A Taoist would say that mixed feelings toward someone close aren’t a broken love but a living one: where there is a deep bond, there is also friction. Trouble begins when we demand a “pure” feeling of ourselves and wage war on its other half. You can let tenderness and irritation flow side by side, like two streams in one river.
ambivalence.practice: Trace the yin-yang circle on your palm with a finger and name one thing about your loved one that gladdens you and one that irritates you. Tell yourself: “Both are true.”

guilty_relief.text: “Better to stop in time than to keep a cup filled to the brim,” Laozi writes (chapter 9): no strain can be sustained forever. Relief after losing someone close, especially after a long illness, often comes together with guilt. Taoism would treat it with great gentleness. There is a well-known story in the Zhuangzi: when Zhuangzi’s wife died, a friend found him sitting and drumming on a bowl. Zhuangzi explained that at first he had grieved like everyone, but then he saw that her life and death were part of the same transformation as the turning of the seasons (chapter 18). This story shouldn’t be read as advice not to grieve. But it shows that a mixture of different feelings at the edge of life is natural. Laozi might say that relief is a breath out after long strain, not a betrayal of love. You can allow yourself both the breath out and the sorrow.
guilty_relief.practice: Take a few slow breaths out and tell yourself: “It’s all right to breathe out. Love doesn’t leave because of it.”

indifference.text: Nanguo Ziqi sat leaning on his armrest, gazing at the sky, as if he had lost himself; his student was alarmed: can the body really become like dry wood, and the heart like dead ashes? (Zhuangzi, chapter 2). Sometimes something ought to move you, yet inside it is quiet and empty — and Zhuangzi was in no hurry to call that a misfortune. Taoism wouldn’t be alarmed by this state. Laozi wrote that Heaven and Earth “are ruthless” (chapter 5) — not in the sense of cruelty, but in that nature doesn’t act out feelings it doesn’t have. Taoism is wary in general of “proper” feelings — of rules about how one is supposed to feel and react. For a Taoist, indifference is sometimes a winter season of the soul: the field is resting, the sap has gone deep. No one demands flowers in winter. This doesn’t mean you’ve become heartless; feelings can return, like spring, in their own time. For now you can stop hurrying yourself and stop pretending, and simply be honest with what is.
indifference.practice: Sit for five minutes like Ziqi at his armrest — feeling nothing “properly,” acting out nothing. Just look out the window at the sky.

escape.text: When the King of Chu sent envoys to offer Zhuangzi a high post, he kept his eyes on his fishing line and asked: what would a sacred tortoise, kept in a temple chest for three thousand years, rather be — revered bones, or alive and dragging its tail through the mud? The wish to drop everything and run — from your job, your city, your role — is something Taoism understands very well. In legends, many Taoist sages left the capitals for the mountains, and Laozi himself, according to tradition, went off to the west, leaving his book with the keeper of a frontier pass. A Taoist would say that the wish to escape may be the voice of your nature, cramped in a shape that isn’t yours. But Taoism also speaks of wu wei — action without forcing yourself. Sometimes leaving isn’t a leap, but a gradual freeing: less of what’s superfluous, more of what is yours. You can look for the Way right where you are, too.
escape.practice: Remove one superfluous thing from your day today — a meeting, a duty, an open tab — like the tortoise that chose the mud over the chest. A small step toward freedom, not a leap.

quote.text: Your name or your person, which is dearer? Your person or your goods, which is worth more?
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 44 (trans. D. C. Lau)

forbidden_attraction.text: “Do not exalt rare goods, and people will not steal,” Laozi advised rulers (chapter 3). Attraction to someone unavailable or “the wrong person” arises by itself, and Taoism wouldn’t see anything unnatural in it: desires rise uninvited, like the wind. But Laozi drew attention to a particular property of the forbidden: when something is declared rare and unattainable, it begins to beckon more strongly. Laozi might say that you can ask: how much of my attraction is the person themselves, and how much is the pull of unavailability, an image I’ve draped over them? Taoism gives no instructions on what to do and passes no verdicts. It invites you to observe desire as you would watch a river’s current: without damming it and without rushing after it, but seeing where it is moving.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Picture this person as ordinary and available — at breakfast, in a bad mood, by a sink of dirty dishes. Notice what is left of the attraction, and what was the gleam of a “rare good.”

social_anxiety.text: The ancient sages, Laozi wrote, were cautious, as if crossing a stream in winter, and hesitant, as if wary of their neighbors (chapter 15). Shyness and fear of judgment make you shrink, as if under others’ eyes you had to become someone else. Taoism is remarkably gentle with this state. There is no reproach in Laozi’s words: caution here looks like sensitivity. The Taoist sages in the Zhuangzi are often inconspicuous and quiet. Taoism would say you don’t have to be bright and loud; the value of pu — the uncarved block, simplicity — needs no flashy presentation. Fear of judgment feeds on our measuring ourselves against someone else’s yardstick. You can allow yourself to be quiet and to be present in the way that is natural to you.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a get-together, tell yourself: “I’m allowed to be quiet.” Choose one thing that comes naturally to you that you’ll do — listen, smile, ask a question.

uncertainty.text: “Misty and dim!” — this is how Laozi describes the Tao itself, and he adds at once: within this dimness there are images, there are things, there is a seed (chapter 21). Not knowing is unsettling: you want to know what will happen. Taoism is perhaps better than any other school at living with not-knowing. The sage doesn’t pretend to know everything. For a Taoist the world is ceaseless transformation: misfortune grows out of good fortune, good fortune out of misfortune, and no one knows where it ends. Laozi might say that uncertainty isn’t a breakdown but the ordinary weather of the Way. You can meet it not by tensing up, but with flexibility, the way a young tree meets the wind: bending, adapting, taking the next step as the road becomes clearer. You don’t have to see the whole trail — it’s enough to see where to put your foot now.
uncertainty.practice: Walk slowly, looking only at the next step, as if in fog. Say to yourself: “I don’t know how things will turn out. But here is the next step.”

waiting.text: Who can let muddy water stand still so that it becomes clear by itself? Laozi asks in chapter 15. Waiting — for an answer, for results, for news — is like standing before a closed door: there’s nothing you can do, and yet you can’t settle down. Taoism knows how to value pauses. Water isn’t cleared by being stirred — only by being allowed to settle. For a Taoist, waiting is a time of wu wei, non-action: not inaction, but giving up needless effort where it changes nothing. Checking your email for the tenth time is like stirring the water again. You can let events ripen at their own pace, and let yourself tend to what is growing right now: a meal, a walk, a conversation.
waiting.practice: While you wait, tend to something that is growing right now: water a plant, cook a meal, go for a walk. Put the phone in another room for that time.

regret.text: “The fish trap exists for the fish: once you’ve caught the fish, you forget the trap,” writes Zhuangzi (chapter 26). Regret over what you did or didn’t do shows that it matters to you how your life has turned out. Taoism would suggest treating the past as material, not as a prison. The same line goes on: the snare exists for the rabbit — once you’ve caught the rabbit, you forget the snare. A Taoist would say that a painful memory is such a trap too: its point lies in the lesson it brings. Once the lesson is caught, you can stop clutching the trap itself. Taoism doesn’t promise that everything worked out for the best, but it reminds you: life is a flow of transformations, and no moment in it is the last. The past is like yesterday’s water in a river: it was there, and the river flows on.
regret.practice: Write down in one line what lesson the situation you regret has brought. Imagine that this is the “fish,” and the rest can be set aside like an unneeded trap.

longing.text: The mason of Ying could slice a speck of plaster, thin as a fly’s wing, off his friend’s nose with one swing of his axe; when his friend was gone, the mason never did it again — Zhuangzi told this story at Huizi’s grave. Longing for a particular person is an aching feeling that stretches like a thread. Since Huizi, his friend and eternal sparring partner, had gone, Zhuangzi said, he had no one left to talk with (chapter 24). Even the sage who taught how to accept change lightly missed a living companion in conversation. Laozi might say that longing is a natural movement of the heart, like the turning of the seasons. You don’t have to hold on to it or chase it away; you can let it flow. The Taoists saw bonds between people as part of the common Way: what was between you has become part of your nature and lives on in how you see the world.
longing.practice: Recall one phrase or habit of this person’s that has stayed with you. Live one moment today “with them” — the way they would have done it.

world_pain.text: Laozi wrote that even a victory in war should be met with the rites of mourning, like a funeral (chapter 31). Pain for the world — heavy news, wars, injustice — is a sign that you feel connected with all living things. Taoism was born in an age of drawn-out wars, and many pages of the Tao Te Ching are full of bitterness about violence. Taoism doesn’t suggest turning away. But it reminds you of measure. Laozi spoke of the “three treasures”: compassion, frugality and humility (chapter 67). Frugality applies to your strength too. Taoism would say you can carry pain for the world without trying to hold the whole world on your shoulders. The soft overcomes the hard: quiet kindness and care for those nearby are also part of how the world heals.
world_pain.practice: Choose one small act of care for those around you today. Then give yourself half an hour of quiet without news.

rejection.text: The duck’s legs are short, but lengthen them and it will suffer; the crane’s legs are long, but shorten them and it will grieve (Zhuangzi, chapter 8). A refusal wounds: it seems you’ve been judged “not right.” Taoism would approach this pain through the idea of the natural nature of things. Every creature is good in its own measure, and forcing it to fit someone else’s means maiming it. Laozi might say that another person’s “no” often says that your natures didn’t match, not that something is wrong with you. A duck is no worse than a crane — they are simply different. You can live through rejection as the pain of a mismatch, without turning it into a verdict on yourself. Your shape isn’t a mistake; it is looking for its place.
rejection.practice: Finish the sentence: “In this situation I wasn’t a fit because…” — and check: is this about my worth, or about a mismatch?

abandonment.text: “Whoever grasps, loses,” Laozi wrote; the sage grasps nothing and therefore loses nothing (chapter 64). The fear of being abandoned grips the heart: you want to hold on to the person and get guarantees. Taoism says honestly that in a world of constant transformation there are no guarantees — but it draws not a cold conclusion from this, but a calm one. The harder you squeeze, the more slips away. Like water in a cupped hand: clench it and it runs out; hold it gently and it stays. For a Taoist, the strongest bond is one that has room in it. Taoism also speaks of the root: Laozi called returning to the root stillness (chapter 16). The root is what holds you from within: your nature, your breath, your place in the world. Leaning on it, it is easier to live through the fear that your support will be taken away.
abandonment.practice: Cup your palms as if holding water and stay like that for a minute. Then place your hands on your belly and feel your breath — your “root.”

unrequited.text: The highest good, Laozi wrote, is like water: it benefits all beings and contends with no one (chapter 8). Unrequited love is one of the oldest sufferings: the feeling flows, but no current flows back. Taoism wouldn’t reproach you for it. It would remind you of ci — the gentle, caring love that Laozi named the first of his treasures. Such love resembles the Tao itself, which gives birth and nurtures without claiming or commanding (chapter 51). A Taoist would say that the fact that your love found no answer doesn’t make it meaningless: the capacity to love is part of your nature, and it doesn’t disappear. But Taoism also speaks of wu wei — not forcing the course of things. The other person’s feeling is their own current; it can’t be turned by force. You can let your love be, without demanding an answer, and in time it will find its own channel.
unrequited.practice: Do one kind thing today, like water — telling no one and expecting no answer: water someone else’s flower, help a stranger. The tenderness this love awakened keeps on flowing.

humiliation.text: Rivers and seas become kings of a hundred valleys because they know how to lie lower than them, writes Laozi (chapter 66). Humiliation burns: it seems you’ve been put lower than everyone. Taoism looks at high and low in an unusual way. Laozi wrote that water, settling in the low places people scorn, is closest to the Tao (chapter 8). For a Taoist, being “below” doesn’t strip you of dignity. What’s more, Laozi pointed out that both being raised up and being humbled keep a person equally anxious, as long as they depend on someone else’s favor. Freedom lies not in regaining the “top,” but in ceasing to measure yourself by this ladder. The pain of humiliation is real, but it speaks of the other person’s action, not of your nature.
humiliation.practice: Picture water flowing downward and remaining water all the same. Tell yourself: “Wherever I end up, I remain myself.”

quote.text: Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared.
quote.author: Laozi

body_shame.text: Crippled Shu was so twisted that his chin was hidden against his navel and his shoulders rose above the top of his head — and yet he fed ten people and lived out the years allotted to him (Zhuangzi, chapter 4). Dissatisfaction with your body is often born of comparison with an ideal, and Taoism is suspicious of ideals. The Zhuangzi has many heroes with unusual bodies. People missing a leg or with strange looks drew others to them so strongly that those others stopped noticing their appearance: when inner power is great, form is forgotten (chapter 5). Laozi might say that the body is part of nature, like a tree or a stone: it has its own shape and its own path, and it doesn’t need to be forced to fit someone else’s yardstick. You can treat it as a living, changing being, not as a project that is forever unfinished.
body_shame.practice: Place your palm on the part of your body you’re used to criticizing, and think of it as part of nature — a branch, a stone, a wave. Keep your hand there for a few breaths.

illness.text: Ziyu, bent by sickness so badly that his back rose into a hump, hobbled to a well, looked at his reflection and said with curiosity: “What is the Creator turning me into?” (Zhuangzi, chapter 6). When the body lets you down, it’s frightening and exhausting. Taoism treats the body as part of nature — with its own ebbs and flows. A friend asked Ziyu whether his illness troubled him; he answered that it didn’t. This isn’t a call to ignore pain, but an image of a courage that accepts change without waging war on oneself. For a Taoist, the body doesn’t need to be “defeated”; you can be its companion — listen to its rhythm, conserve your strength the way water conserves its own, flowing around stones. Illness isn’t your fault or your failure, but a difficult stretch of the Way.
illness.practice: Ask your body: “What do you need right now?” — and listen for the first answer: warmth, rest, water, quiet. Give it one of these.

pride.text: Having finished carving up the ox, Cook Ding stood with his knife in hand, looked all around, lingered, pleased with himself — and then wiped the knife and put it away (Zhuangzi, chapter 3). Pride in something you’ve done is a good, well-earned feeling. Taoism doesn’t demand that you hide it, but it suggests a particular way of carrying it. Laozi describes the Tao as creating without claiming, accomplishing without boasting. When the sage has finished a task, they step aside — not out of false modesty, but because the work now lives its own life. A Taoist would say that healthy pride is like the quiet joy of a master craftsman. Cook Ding isn’t bragging — he is savoring what he has done. You can allow yourself this moment: pause, look around and be glad — without competition and without needing an audience.
pride.practice: Pause for a minute, like Cook Ding: look back at what you’ve done and allow yourself to be pleased — without judgments or comparisons.

quote.text: Retire when the task is accomplished. This is the way of heaven.
quote.author: Laozi
quote.source: Tao Te Ching, 9 (trans. D. C. Lau)

melancholy.text: Tao Yuanming, the poet who left his official post for the sake of his garden, wrote: “I pick chrysanthemums by the eastern fence, and far off, silent, the Southern Mountains rise.” Bright sadness is a quiet feeling that holds both sorrow and beauty. Taoism is perhaps closest of all to it: it sees life as ceaseless transformation, where everything comes and goes like clouds over mountains. In Chinese poetry, which grew up alongside Taoism, bright sadness is a frequent guest: autumn leaves, the moon over a river, a solitary crane. Laozi might say that melancholy can be understood as the yin of the soul — the cool, quiet, inward-turned side, without which there is no yang either. There’s no need to drive it away. Zhuangzi wrote that joy and sorrow follow one another like day and night. Evening is no worse than morning — it just has a different light. You can allow yourself this evening.
melancholy.practice: Sit by a window or step outside for a few minutes and watch something slow — clouds, light, leaves. Just be with it.
